cim: Guest commentary: Artificial intelligence is inflating medical bills
cim_eredeti: Guest commentary: Artificial intelligence is inflating medical bills
szoveg_eredeti:
Just when the healthcare system seemed as complicated as it could get, artificial intelligence has stepped in to introduce a new set of hurdles.

Medical debt in particular appears to be one of those hurdles set to become even harder to overcome.

Consider two study reports published this year:

An Oct. 6 study by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation found more than one in four adults, 27%, reported they or a member of their family had medical debt in December 2025; and a J.P. Morgan report on Aug. 17 that identified “early wins in revenue cycle management, patient triage, prior authorization, and billing.”

Between the two it’s clear who stands to lose and who to profit the most with the increasing deployment of AI innovation in healthcare.

Companies like Cedar, an AI-powered healthcare billing platform, which provides a “payment experience, personalized to each patient,” are already changing the way providers use technology to bill and tailor payments by patients.

And, a report by BlueCross Blue Shield in March found significant cases of “AI upcoding” across claims data from tens of thousands of maternity admissions, which added $22 million to maternity admission costs in one year.

AI-driven upcoding refers to an increasing of diagnosis complexity that allows the hospital to bill insurance companies more.

AI tools, marketed as transformative for healthcare, are also making it easier to inflate the cost of care.

This presents a new challenge for hospitals, especially nonprofit hospitals, seeking to automate and optimize patient billing.

With each passing day, we seem to be squeezing more of the “AI toothpaste” out of the tube, which makes even the suggestion of a ban on AI deployment in healthcare organizations unrealistic.

The next best thing would be to establish clear rules on how AI can be used.

To begin with, hospitals need to screen patients for financial assistance before utilizing automated billing systems that seem to be programmed by a “collect first, ask questions later” modus operandi.

An investigation by Tradeoffs, a nonprofit news organization reporting on healthcare systems, examined the presumptive eligibility policies of 166 nonprofit hospitals and found that in Texas 44% often billed patients before screening them for free or discounted care.

The increasing use of AI to not just bill patients but also personalize payments is compounding a problem that already exists.

Personalization may not by default be discriminatory. However, the likelihood of AI-powered billing operating transparently is a separate and potentially more dangerous prospect.

The Texas Health and Safety Code, Sec 185.002 already requires healthcare providers to submit itemized bills for each service and supply provided to the patient during a visit and in a plain language description.

The real innovation in AI-powered healthcare would be for hospitals to utilize algorithms that strengthen legal protections, not create loopholes that allow them to defer responsibility to the algorithm.

Dr. Jarrel De Matas is an assistant professor at the University of Texas Medical Branch.
